newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh leader gets tough on ministers, officials.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh leader gets tough on ministers, officials.

text.p: Kazakh President Nursultan Nazarbayev has urged his government to crack down on wage arrears and speed up reforms, threatening tough measures against officials who do not measure up.

"The issue of unpaid pensions and salaries is becoming a political issue...The tempo of reforms is becoming slower, amd the social-political situation is aggravating," Nazarbayev told a special meeting of the government and regional bosses.
The meeting, on Monday, was closed to foreign media, but extracts were shown on television late in the evening.
Nazarbayev said the government and regional heads had to solve the problems by April 1. "I warn you, this is becoming very serious," he thundered.
He ordered officials to report back in April and said some could be ousted if they did not perform satisfactorily.
"Some members of the government could be given the sack right in this hall...The patience of Kazakh citizens has its limits," he said.
The government estimates debts on salaries and pensions at 60 billion tenge ($792 million).

Finance Minister Alexander Pavlov, defending his policies, said companies simply did not have money on their accounts to pay wages. He has said that over 40 percent of Kazakh companies were potential bankrupts.
Nazarbayev also said Kazakhstan had to accelerate its privatisation campaign, a sell-off of state property which is already way behind target.
The government sold just 62 companies of the 194 slated for cash privatisation last year.

Voucher privatisation was also slow and some 67 percent of Kazakhs swapped privatisation vouchers for shares in just 1,768 companies, compared to the 7,000 companies originally listed when the campaign started in 1994.

The authorities have said they pin their hopes for Kazakhstan's economic revival on sell-offs of large companies in the energy sector, communications and in extraction and processing of rich natural resources.
Nazarbayev promised to channel $175 million in loans from the Asian Bank for Development, Japan's ExImbank and the budget to help small and medium-sized business.
